title: Jeremiah 40:1–6
context: Jeremiah 40:1–6 opens with a heading, “The word which came to Jeremiah from the LORD”, followed by a narrative rather than an immediate oracle; readers differ on whether the heading introduces the whole section that follows or a word that comes later. The narrator says that Nebuzaradan let Jeremiah go from Ramah, after he had been taken in chains among the captives (40:1); how this relates to 39:14 and 38:28 is left unresolved here. Ramah lay north of Jerusalem and is commonly thought to have served as a gathering point for the captives, though this is an inference (compare 31:15). Nebuzaradan then says, “The LORD your God pronounced this evil on this place; and the LORD has brought it” (40:2–3), and says it came because the people sinned against the LORD. It is striking that a Babylonian officer voices the judgment Jeremiah had preached; readers suggest that he had heard Jeremiah’s message reported, that he speaks in the idiom of the conquered people, or that the narrator shapes his words, and these notes do not settle the question. Nebuzaradan releases Jeremiah from his chains and offers him a choice: to come to Babylon under his care, or to stay, perhaps with Gedaliah, whom the king of Babylon has made governor (40:4–5). He gives Jeremiah food and a present (40:5). Jeremiah goes to Gedaliah at Mizpah and lives with him among the people who were left in the land (40:6). The narrator does not say why Jeremiah chose to stay, and these notes do not speculate. Mizpah lay in Benjamin north of Jerusalem; its exact site is commonly identified but not certain.

verses.text: The word which came to Jeremiah from the LORD, after Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had let him go from Ramah, when he had taken him being bound in chains among all the captives of Jerusalem and Judah who were carried away captive to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator introduces “The word which came to Jeremiah from the LORD” and then tells how Nebuzaradan let him go from Ramah after he had been bound in chains among the captives. Arminian readers note that the heading is followed by narrative, and they leave open which word it introduces.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same question about the heading and the relation of this release at Ramah to 39:14 and 38:28. They do not harmonize the accounts, and they observe that Ramah, north of Jerusalem, is commonly taken as a gathering point for captives, though this is inferred.

verses.text: The captain of the guard took Jeremiah and said to him, “The LORD your God pronounced this evil on this place;
verses.arminianNotes: The captain of the guard said to Jeremiah, “The LORD your God pronounced this evil on this place”. Arminian readers find it striking that a Babylonian officer speaks of the LORD’s judgment, and they hold open whether he repeats what he had heard of Jeremiah’s message or the narrator shapes his words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise find the speech striking and hedge its source. They note that God’s judgment is confessed even from the mouth of a foreign officer, and they point to the existing box at Judges 9:23 for how the traditions describe God’s use of Babylon, without reopening it.

verses.text: and the LORD has brought it, and done according as he spoke. Because you have sinned against the LORD, and have not obeyed his voice, therefore this thing has come on you.
verses.arminianNotes: Nebuzaradan says the LORD has done as he spoke, because the people sinned against him and did not obey his voice. Arminian readers note that the verdict on Judah’s disobedience matches Jeremiah’s preaching, and they see the irony of a foreigner explaining Judah’s ruin to the prophet who had warned them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same irony and observe that the words this thing has come on you speak to the people as a whole. They read the speech as confirming that the fall of Jerusalem was not chance but the outcome of God’s spoken word, a conviction both traditions share.

verses.text: Now, behold, I release you today from the chains which are on your hand. If it seems good to you to come with me into Babylon, come, and I will take care of you; but if it seems bad to you to come with me into Babylon, don’t. Behold, all the land is before you. Where it seems good and right to you to go, go there.”
verses.arminianNotes: Nebuzaradan releases Jeremiah from his chains and offers him the choice to come to Babylon under his care or to go wherever seems good to him. Arminian readers note the real freedom given to the prophet, and they read the offer simply as reported without inferring more than the text says.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jeremiah’s freedom here comes through a Babylonian officer, a further sign of God’s care for him. They observe that the text gives the offer in detail but does not reveal Jeremiah’s thoughts about it, and they leave his reasons unstated as the text does.

verses.text: Now while he had not yet gone back, “Go back then,” he said, “to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon has made governor over the cities of Judah, and dwell with him among the people; or go wherever it seems right to you to go.” So the captain of the guard gave him food and a present, and let him go.
verses.arminianNotes: Nebuzaradan tells Jeremiah he may go back to Gedaliah, whom the king of Babylon has made governor, or go wherever seems right to him, and gives him food and a present. Arminian readers note the kindness shown to the prophet, and they see God providing for his servant through an unexpected source.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same provision and observe that the appointment of Gedaliah gives a measure of order to the remnant left in the land. They read the gifts of food and a present as part of the way the LORD kept his promise to protect Jeremiah through the fall of the city.

verses.text: Then Jeremiah went to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam to Mizpah, and lived with him among the people who were left in the land.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah went to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam at Mizpah and lived with him among the people who were left in the land. Arminian readers report the choice as the text gives it, noting that Jeremiah remained among the remnant, and they do not speculate about his motives, which the narrator does not state.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise report Jeremiah’s choice without guessing at his reasons. They note that Mizpah lay in Benjamin, north of Jerusalem, though its exact site is not certain, and they read the verse as placing the prophet among the people who remained in the land after the exile.
